synopsis: PAEB detects people on foot and brakes for them; the corpus identifies pedestrians as the main people heavy off-road CMS must protect, while describing pedestrian detection as especially condition-dependent [f11688, f11696, f11698]. FMVSS 127 requires pedestrian AEB at 10–73 km/h in daylight and darkness, but applies to light on-road vehicles up to 4,536 kg GVWR, not off-road machines; Chapter 3 states UN R152 pedestrian tests use 20–60 km/h while also flagging that range as unverified against primary text [f11691, f2831, f2824, f2528]. A peer-reviewed 2019 retrospective on-road simulation evaluated time-to-collision triggers and latencies against US pedestrian crash data, showing that avoidance depends on both parameters [f6346, f6189]. Independent nighttime tests improved from no avoidance by four vehicles at 25 mph in 2019 to 60% avoidance in the study published 16 October 2025, which tested four recent cars at 40 km/h and still left roughly 40% failures under ideal conditions [f7975, f7976, f7977]. High-visibility clothing caused complete detection loss in some tested systems, and nighttime and clothing conditions were under-represented in consumer protocols, demonstrating that protocol-based evidence can give false confidence outside its tested envelope [f7980, f7981, f7982]. Because job-site pedestrians wear high-visibility clothing and much work occurs at night, the corpus recommends retaining physical night and weather tests where simulation is weakest; Caterpillar also warns of detection limitations for crouching or lying people, low light and inclement weather [f11697, f11699, f11695].
